newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary business ethics questioned after scandals.
newsitem.headline: Hungary business ethics questioned after scandals.

text.p: Scandals at Hungary's central bank and the country's privatisation agency have put a spotlight on the performance and probity of post-communist bureaucrats.

Central bank chief Gyorgy Suranyi on Tuesday sought to divorce the resignation of two of his vice presidents over an options deal gone wrong from a scandal over irregular payments in the state privatisation agency APV Rt.
"A very deep and clear differentiation between this case and another case which occupies the public opinion must be made," Suranyi told reporters.
But in the minds of analysts trying to plot the course of Hungary's emerging economy, the two problems reflect the strains on the competence and probity of government officials.

"They are victims in an indirect way as there is now a general intolerance against executives in the public sector," analyst Tibor Vidos of GJW Consult said of the two central bankers who resigned over a botched options trade.

NBH vice presidents Frigyes Harshegyi and Sandor Czirjak announced their official resignations on Tuesday morning after disclosure of an unfavourable foreign exchange contract with Creditanstalt Investment Fund, concluded in 1992, that could cost the NBH hundreds more than three billion forints ($19 million).
The contract, for foreign exchange rate guarantees maturing in 1998, forced the NBH to create substantial risk reserves that have proven extremely costly.

Nevertheless, Suranyi said the vice presidents had contributed substantially to the improvement of the NBH's picture in Hungary and abroad and as such, he urged Prime Minister Gyula Horn not to accept their resignation.
"I recommended him not to accept the resignation offers, or at least not with an effect which is so close," Suranyi said.
Though no on one is suggesting any illegality in the central bank case, it has came on the heels of a more serious scandal involving the APV Rt.
Irregular payments of millions of dollars from the APV to a consultant, Marta Tocsik, led to the dismissal of the entire APV board and the minister in charge.
Because of the proximity of the two cases, political analyst Attila Ledenyi said he believed the government was under pressure to take any whiff of scandal extremely seriously.
"The government feels it is important that people who make mistakes should resign so they overplayed this one. Otherwise it seems ridicilous to bring things up from years ago," he said.
Vidos said the general climate could eventually harm the image of the government abroad but added that there were signs the worst may be over.
"The APV's new board is up and running and things are getting back to normal," Vidos said.
The government said on Monday the new board would hold its first meeting on Wednesday.
Vidos also said new privatisation minister Judit Csiha seemed more ready than her predecessor, Tamas Suchman, to allow the management to get on with its job.
On Tuesday, Parliament confirmed Csiha as privatisation minister and Szabolcs Fazakas as minister of trade, industry and tourism, replacing Suchman who held both portfolios.
Csiha told reporters upon her appointment that she was determined that privatisation would continue interrupted.
"The government is determined that the process of privatisation must be continued," she said. "One cannot and should not expect a change in strategy which would weaken or reverse this philosophy."
She also announced the setting up of a committee to examine all contracts entered into by APV.
Vidos added new APV board chairman Arpad Kovacs's record as State Audit Office head would ensure rules are adhered to.
Ledenyi also saw public interest in the APV case waning and said Western investors would be more concerned about consistent government policy. ($1=159.16 Forint)
